cards.text: Job lost his children and his wealth (Job 1:13-19), and then his health (Job 2:7). He just sat through a long speech from his friend Eliphaz the Temanite (Job 2:11; 4:1-5:27). Now it's Job's turn to answer, and friend, he has a LOT to say.
Job starts with a wish. If only his grief and his calamity could be put on the scales together.

cards.question: Job says his grief would outweigh the sand of the seas. What does he say that explains?

answers.text: Why his words have been rash
Why he sent his friends away

cards.text: Then Job says arrows have pierced him, and his spirit drinks in their poison.

cards.question: Job says arrows have pierced him and poisoned his spirit. Whose arrows does he say they are?

cards.text: Next, Job asks about animals. Does a wild donkey bray over fresh grass, or an ox low over its fodder? Friend, a donkey with fresh grass has NOTHING to complain about.

Then he asks if tasteless food is eaten without salt, or if there's any flavor in the white of an egg. I forgot the sugar in a batch once. ONE batch. Baker, those cookies tasted like cardboard that gave up on its dreams.

cards.question: Tasteless food without salt, the white of an egg. Job says he'd gladly eat food like that.

cards.text: Then Job says he has a request, and he hopes God will grant it. Friend, this one is heavy.

cards.question: Job has a heavy request for God. What does he hope God will be willing to do?

answers.text: Crush him and cut him off
Give back all that he lost

cards.question: Even through unrelenting pain, Job says one thing still brings him comfort and joy. What is it?

answers.text: He has not denied the Holy One's words
His health is slowly getting better
His wealth will soon be returned

cards.text: Then Job asks what strength he has that he should still hope, and what future he has that he should be patient.

cards.question: Job says his strength is like stone and his flesh is made of bronze.
Job asks if there's any help left within him. What does he say has been driven from him?

cards.text: Now Job turns from his own pain to his friends. He has something to say about what a man in despair should get from a friend.

cards.question: Job says a despairing man should have the ___ of his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty.

cards.text: Then Job paints a picture. He says his brothers are as faithless as wadis, seasonal streams that overflow with ice and melting snow.

cards.question: Wadis overflow when the snow melts. What does Job say happens to them in the dry season?

cards.text: Caravans turn aside from their routes into the wasteland. The caravans of Tema look for water, and the travelers of Sheba hope to find it.

cards.question: The caravans of Tema and Sheba come to the wadis hoping for water. What does their arrival bring?

cards.text: Job says it plainly: right now his friends are no help. Baker, it's the buddy who says, "Call me ANYTIME." So you call. Straight. To. Voicemail.

cards.question: Job tells his friends that when they see terror, they are afraid.

cards.text: Then Job asks his friends a question about what he's ever asked them for.

cards.question: Job says he once asked his friends for a bribe from their wealth to rescue him.

cards.text: So what does Job want from his friends? He says, “Teach me, and I will be silent.”

cards.question: Job asks his friends to teach him. What does he ask them to help him understand?

cards.text: Job says, “How painful are honest words!” Then he asks what their argument even proves.

cards.question: Job asks if his friends intend to correct his words. What else does he ask if they'll treat as wind?

cards.text: Job says they'd even cast lots for an orphan and barter away their friend. Then he says, “But now, please look at me. Would I lie to your face?”

cards.question: Job asks his friends to reconsider and not be unjust. What does he say is at stake?

cards.text: Now Job zooms out to everybody. He says man's days are like a hired hand's, like a slave longing for shade, like a hireling waiting for his wages. Every adult knows that Thursday-before-payday feeling.

cards.question: Job compares himself to a hired hand waiting on wages. What does he say he's been allotted?

cards.text: When Job lies down, he thinks, “When will I get up?” Baker, you know the night before a big early flight? Staring at the ceiling, checking the clock every twenty minutes? THAT.

cards.question: The night drags on for Job. What does he do until dawn?

cards.text: Job describes his body: worms, dirt, and skin cracked and festering. And his days are flying by, swifter than a weaver's shuttle.

cards.question: Job says his days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle. How does he say they come to an end?
Job says his life is but a breath, but his eyes will see happiness again someday.

cards.text: Job says, “You will look for me, but I will be no more.” Like a cloud that vanishes, the one who goes down to Sheol does not come back up.

cards.question: Job says the one who goes down to Sheol never returns to his house. What does he say about that man's place?
After all that, Job decides to hold his tongue and keep the anguish of his spirit to himself.

cards.text: Then Job speaks straight to God. He asks whether he is the sea, or the monster of the deep.

cards.question: Job asks God if he is the sea or the monster of the deep. What does Job say God must do to him?

cards.text: Job hopes his bed will comfort him. Instead, he says, God frightens him with dreams and terrifies him with visions.

cards.question: Job says those dreams and visions are so terrifying that he would prefer death over his life in this body.

cards.text: “I loathe my life!” Job says. He would not live forever, and he asks to be left alone, because his days are but a breath.
Then Job asks God, “What is man that You should exalt him, that You should set Your heart upon him,” that You check on him every morning and test him every moment?

cards.question: Job feels tested every moment. What does he ask God?

answers.text: Whether God will ever look away
Whether God will send him rain

cards.question: Job calls God “O watcher of mankind.” Then he asks why God has made him something. What?
Near the end, Job asks God why He does not pardon his transgression and take away his iniquity.

cards.text: Job ends by saying he'll soon lie down in the dust, and God will seek him, but he'll be no more. That's where we leave it for now, friend. Trust me, this conversation is far from over.

findings.problem: Stop 3, card 18 quotes "O watcher of mankind.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The setup line "Friend, this one is heavy" rules out the wrong answer "Give back all that he lost" on card 10. That answer isn't heavy, so the line points the baker toward the death wish.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The right answer, "He has not denied the Holy One's words," is the only one in Bible wording. The two wrong answers are plain modern statements, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: Nothing earlier lets the baker reason that "success" is what was driven from Job rather than wisdom or courage. The baker has to guess the wording of the line.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop: 5 multiple choice, 2 true or false, 0 fill in the blank.

rule.text: Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "correction" can be argued right. In 6:24 Job asks his friends, "Teach me... Help me understand how I have erred."

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The card cites Job 6:18 but leaves out that the caravans go into the wasteland and perish. That is the high point of Job's picture of friends who fail.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: "Job feels tested every moment" states Job's feeling as a fact. In 7:18 he says God tests man every moment. That is something he says, not a feeling the text gives him.

rule.text: Feelings: He can guess at a feeling, marked as his own ("I think," "I bet"). Never as fact.
